clue.text: The monstrous regiment carried the day without me

indicators.note: without is used in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: to carry the day is to win, and this is the past tense
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fearsome army unit won a battle without the speaker's help.
explanation.walkthrough: WO(ME)N. John Knox's 1558 pamphlet attacked female rulers as 'the monstrous regiment of women', and the phrase stuck.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a famous quotation from Knox, whose title ends with that very word, so it serves as a literary allusion.

clue.text: Jonah couldn't have given it you, alas!

parts.words: Jonah couldn't have given it you
parts.note: surface reading: the biblical prophet, whose presence aboard brought a storm, could not have been more unlucky company
setter's reading: a Jonah is a jinx, and the most a jinx can bring you is a worsened fortune, which is also a phrase meaning alas

explanation.walkthrough: A Jonah is sailors' slang for someone who brings bad luck, after the prophet thrown overboard to calm the storm.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-word phrase is an everyday exclamation of regret, used exactly where one might sigh and say alas.

clue.text: Doctor, we need the right cutting implement

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, an army doctor
taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A surgeon asks for the proper instrument for an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like an anagram signal, but here it is simply MO.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine with blades for trimming grass on a lawn is a tool for cutting, so it counts as a cutting implement.

clue.text: Jones is a near one!

parts.note: surface reading: someone called Jones narrowly avoided something, as in a near thing
setter's reading: the Joneses are the family next door you try to keep up with, so Jones is a person who lives near you

explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping up with the Joneses' means trying to match the lifestyle of the people next door.
explanation.definitionFit: The person living next door or nearby is literally the one near you, which the idiom about the Joneses makes Jones.

clue.text: Try to complete flight

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a score in rugby, or its equivalent in American football
second meaning: the landing of an aircraft at the end of its journey

explanation.surface: An instruction to attempt finishing a journey by air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' looks like a verb meaning attempt; it is a noun, the rugby score.
explanation.definitionFit: Grounding the ball scores in rugby, and an aircraft landing on the runway ends its journey; both share the same phrase.

clue.text: Lever that's altered in some way

indicators.note: the word before has been changed in some manner, so its letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lever that has been modified somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altered' reads like part of the signal, but it is the fodder; 'in some way' tells you to shuffle it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a foot-operated lever that drives a machine such as an old sewing machine or a potter's wheel.

clue.text: Raises some food for one newly arrived

parts.note: to up something is to raise it, so this is the third-person verb
a tart is one kind of food, a pastry

explanation.surface: Someone lifts a plate of food for a newcomer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a person who has risen suddenly to importance, a parvenu or arriviste who has only just arrived.

clue.text: Crude dwelling (place by saltwater lake

parts.note: Hove is a seaside town on the English south coast, next to Brighton
L is the abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A rough hut stands at a coastal spot beside a salt lagoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray bracket is a scanning error in the newspaper copy.
explanation.definitionFit: A small squalid hut or shack is a rough, primitive home, which is what a crude dwelling describes.

clue.text: Pro's one up — blunders deliberately

indicators.note: something that blunders goes wrong, so these letters are jumbled out of order

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A professional golfer, leading by a stroke, makes mistakes on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: A pro deliberately blundering suggests match-fixing, which makes the definition fit the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means intentionally, with a set aim in mind, which is the same as doing something deliberately.

clue.text: Look after union's employees, primarily

parts.note: the NUR was the National Union of Railwaymen, plus S for the possessive

indicators.note: primarily points to what comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of employees

explanation.surface: Care for the workers belonging to a trade union, first and foremost.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUR was a large British rail workers' union in the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse someone or something is to tend it with care, which is to look after it.

clue.text: Rumpus and ruckus reach their ultimate, we hear, in disorderly conduct

parts.note: a row is a noisy quarrel, a rumpus
a din is a loud racket, a ruckus

indicators.note: we hear says a letter is to be written as it is spoken aloud, not as its symbol

parts.note: the last letter of both rumpus and ruckus is S, spelt out as the name of the letter

explanation.surface: A noisy disturbance escalates until it reaches its peak in rowdy behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reach their ultimate' looks like climax, but it means the final letter of the two words, S, written as its spoken name.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough, noisy, boisterous behaviour is what the noun describes, so it matches unruly conduct exactly.

clue.text: Treacherous person, but one important to a ruler

parts.note: a VIP is a very important person
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A traitor who is nevertheless valuable to the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A snake is a common figurative term for someone spiteful or treacherous, a viper in the bosom.

clue.text: In 23 it is shifted by' bulldozers

indicators.note: shifted means moved about, so the letters of the referenced answer are rearranged

parts.note: the answer to 23 across

explanation.surface: Something that bulldozers push around on a building site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shifted' does double duty: it shuffles the letters of 23 and describes what bulldozers do. The stray apostrophe is a scanning error.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulldozers exist to move soil and ground about, so the material they push is the stuff described.

clue.text: Making girl more accomplished, that's magic

parts.note: Di is a short girl's name
abler means more capable
i.e. is short for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Turning a girl into someone more skilled sounds like a magic trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word means sorcery or black magic, literally devilry, the work of a diable or devil.

clue.text: Free from constraint — light by implication?

parts.note: surface reading: a plain definition, to release or set free
setter's reading: loose is a sense of light (as in a light or loose woman), and the word implies that sense despite its negating prefix, which here adds nothing

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the un- prefix ought to reverse loose, yet the word means the same as loose.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to unfasten or release, setting something free from whatever was holding it in.

clue.text: Eighty winks? Not to start with, thirteen

parts.note: forty winks is a nap, so twice that is an extended nap

indicators.note: to start with points to the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the first letter of not

explanation.surface: A long sleep, but not at first, comes to thirteen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not to start with' looks like an instruction to drop a first letter; it simply takes the N of 'Not'.
explanation.definitionFit: A baker's dozen is thirteen, and the phrase is another name for a dozen plus one extra.

clue.text: Dominant leader interrupts in excessive way

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so one piece is placed in the middle of another

parts.note: too means to an excessive degree
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
the PM, Prime Minister, is the country's leader

explanation.surface: A dominant leader butts in in an overbearing manner.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion lands between the two Os, splitting the excessive word rather than sitting between the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Something uppermost or highest in rank is dominant, in the sense of being above all others.

clue.text: Drink, then a row — the end of the story

parts.note: punch is a mixed drink, served from a bowl
a line is a row of things

explanation.surface: A drink, then a quarrel: how many a night out ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a row' suggests a quarrel, but it means a line of things.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the final line of a joke, which delivers the laugh at the very close of the tale.

clue.text: Latest bit of equipment, man says, is US

indicators.note: the latest bit of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of equipment
he is a male pronoun
to state is to say

explanation.surface: A man announces that the newest gadget is American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' looks like the pronoun us, but it is the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans and others commonly call their country by this informal name, short for the United States.

clue.text: Relations of a sort with revolutionary

parts.note: a kind is a sort or type
a red is a communist, a revolutionary

explanation.surface: Family members of a certain type who share radical politics.
explanation.definitionFit: As a plural noun, the word means family and blood relatives, one's kin.

clue.text: When it's dry long grass of course gets covered in dust outside

indicators.note: getting covered means being enclosed, so one piece goes inside the other
outside points to the outer letters of the word before it, the first and last

parts.note: the outer letters of dust
on a golf course the rough is the area of long grass beside the fairway

explanation.surface: In dry weather long grass gets covered with dust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as naturally, but it means of a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a long period without rain, a time of dryness, which the phrase describes.

clue.text: Admit defeat against one of the top players, we hear

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: we hear means the piece is spelt as a word that sounds the same, not its own spelling

parts.note: in tennis a seed is a ranked top player

explanation.surface: Losing to a leading tennis player and conceding the match.
explanation.definitionFit: To concede is to yield or acknowledge that one has lost, so it is to admit defeat.

clue.text: Players went ahead, having moved two men

parts.note: the cast are the players in a play
led means was in front, went ahead

explanation.surface: Players advanced after moving two pieces, as in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess castling is the one move that shifts two pieces at once, king and rook.
explanation.definitionFit: Castling moves the king and a rook together, so a player who did it has shifted two chessmen in one turn.

clue.text: One thus might appear ridiculous

parts.note: surface reading: a person behaving this way may look silly
setter's reading: add one (I) to the answer's letters and rearrange them, and they appear as the word ridiculous

explanation.walkthrough: The answer and 'ridiculous' share every letter but one I, so the clue is both a definition and a letter hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean absurd and laughable, so the answer is a straight synonym of the last word.

clue.text: Cyril's moving words

indicators.note: moving means the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: the five letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Cyril speaks touchingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' looks like an adjective meaning touching; it signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The singular can stand for the text of a song, and lyrics are the words set to music.

clue.text: Leader of rebellion? Leader of rebellion's inside a cell

indicators.note: inside means placed within, so one piece goes in the middle of the other

parts.note: Jack Cade led a peasants' revolt in Kent in 1450

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of rebellion

explanation.surface: The ringleader of an uprising is locked up inside a prison cell.
explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase is read twice: first as a historical rebel, then as the first letter of 'rebellion'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small core group of activists or trained personnel forms a unit, like a political cell within a movement.

clue.text: Spirit featured in the Arthurian legends

indicators.note: featured in says the word lies within the letters of the phrase after it

parts.note: the letters run across the first two words; legends completes the surface

explanation.surface: The fighting spirit at the centre of the tales of King Arthur.
explanation.definitionFit: Courage or enthusiasm is spirit, and having this in a fight means having courage and determination.

clue.text: Collect featured in a service

parts.note: taken as written
Mass is a church service, the Eucharist

explanation.surface: A collect, a short prayer, is part of a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collect' looks like a noun, the prayer; it is the verb, to gather.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather together a quantity of things, piling them up, is to collect them.

clue.text: Put up, by the sound of it, and knocked down

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word is spelt as one that is said the same way

parts.note: to put something up is to raise it

explanation.surface: A building is erected and then demolished.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the two words sound alike but mean opposites.
explanation.definitionFit: A building razed to the ground has been demolished completely, so it has been knocked down.

clue.text: What Rovers do when game stands about 1-5

indicators.note: standing about something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: game means brave or plucky, as gallant does
1 and 5 in Roman numerals are I and V

explanation.surface: Football fans wait to see how a team called Rovers fares at one-five.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rovers' looks like a football club, and 1-5 a score; rovers are wanderers.
explanation.definitionFit: To roam about in search of fun is what people who wander do, so it describes rovers' activity.

clue.text: With what's in the paper, newspaperman is satisfied

parts.note: the content of a newspaper is what it contains
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor is pleased with the edition's contents.
explanation.definitionFit: Being happy with things as they are, without wanting more, is to be pleased and fulfilled.

clue.text: Lets up and stops short of a hundred

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so the following letter is taken away

parts.note: to cease is to stop
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone eases off and halts just before reaching a century.
explanation.walkthrough: A batsman stopping short of a hundred runs is the cricket picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease off is to slacken or relax, which is what letting up means.
